clothing-001:clothing-01.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. The acknowledged existence of Malaysian celana and more specific compounds does not defeat the everyday celana–seluar contrast.
clothing-001:clothing-01.reason: Celana and seluar are natural contemporary umbrella terms for pants or trousers in Indonesia and Malaysia respectively, and the national contrast is useful. Both can also cover shorter garments, so full length may be expressed as celana panjang or seluar panjang, but that ordinary breadth does not invalidate the card’s stated sense.

clothing-001:clothing-02.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. Dictionary synonymy between kasut and sepatu is not evidence that they are equally preferred in Malaysian everyday usage.
clothing-001:clothing-02.reason: Sepatu is the ordinary Indonesian word for shoes, while kasut is the ordinary Malaysian Malay word. The pairing accurately expresses the same general footwear sense and represents a strong, useful national lexical contrast. Malaysian recognition of sepatu as an Indonesian-associated synonym does not undermine it.

common-verbs-001:everyday-actions-01.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. The overlap of Indonesian antar and Malaysian kirim is ordinary synonymy and semantic overlap, not a reason to reject the principal kirim–hantar contrast.
common-verbs-001:everyday-actions-01.reason: Kirim is natural Indonesian for sending an item, whereas hantar is the normal broad Malaysian verb for sending or delivering one. Malaysian kirim remains available in somewhat narrower or context-dependent uses, but this does not erase the useful everyday contrast. Bare stems are acceptable vocabulary-card forms, although inflected forms are usual in complete formal sentences.

communication-001:communication-01.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. The lack of comparative frequency evidence in the notes is not a material linguistic problem because the contemporary pesan–mesej contrast is well established.
communication-001:communication-01.reason: Pesan is a natural Indonesian noun for an individual written or digital message, while mesej is the usual Malaysian Malay form for that sense. Indonesian pesan is polysemous and Malaysian pesanan can mean a conveyed message, request, or instruction, but neither fact makes the pairing inaccurate.

communication-001:communication-03.concrete_remaining_issue: The sense must distinguish the native words for informal conversation from the shared borrowing chat used especially in digital contexts.

corrections.historical_usage.indonesian.preferred: Obrolan is a natural noun for an informal conversation; chat is often preferred for an app feature or specifically text-based exchange.
corrections.historical_usage.malaysian.preferred: Sembang is a natural Malaysian word for an informal conversation; chat is also very common for specifically online or app-based exchanges.
corrections.sense: an informal or relaxed conversation, whether in person or online

communication-001:communication-03.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. The common use of chat in both countries narrows the contrast but does not eliminate the valid obrolan–sembang distinction for informal conversation generally.
communication-001:communication-03.reason: Obrolan and sembang are natural country-associated words for a casual or informal conversation, so the underlying contrast is worth learning. The present sense overemphasizes text or online chat, where the English borrowing chat is highly natural in both places and may be more idiomatic for an app feature or messaging activity. The card remains usable as a general-conversation contrast but should not imply that these are the uniquely preferred digital terms.

everyday-objects-001:everyday-objects-05.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. Dictionary redirection to “terung” does not outweigh the established everyday Indonesian preference for “terong.”
everyday-objects-001:everyday-objects-05.reason: Both forms accurately denote eggplant. “Terong” is the ordinary contemporary Indonesian form despite “terung” also occurring, while “terung” is the normal Malaysian spelling. The small but systematic form contrast is useful to learners.

everyday-objects-001:everyday-objects-06.reason: “Semangka” and “tembikai” are the normal everyday words for watermelon in Indonesia and Malaysia respectively. The contrast is clear and worth learning.

food-001:foods-01.reason: Both expressions naturally denote lunch or eating lunch. Indonesian normally uses “makan siang,” whereas Malaysian Malay normally uses “makan tengah hari.” Their shared “makan” and parallel phrase structure justify “similar,” while the differing time expression remains useful to learn.

food-001:foods-04.historical_objection_assessment: The objection correctly identifies that the Malaysian description understates “enak.” The cited tourism page alone cannot establish comparative frequency, but the existence of natural Malaysian “enak” usage does not defeat “sedap” as the more characteristic learner default.
food-001:foods-04.reason: “Enak” and “sedap” are excellent default learner answers for Indonesia and Malaysia respectively, and the contrast is worth learning. However, Malaysian “enak” is not merely understood: it is also natural contemporary Malay for tasty food, although “sedap” is generally the more characteristic everyday choice.

food-001:foods-06.historical_objection_assessment: The objections demand stronger comparative evidence than this straightforward spelling contrast requires. The examples and ordinary usage support the meanings; lack of direct comparison with broader alternatives such as “kue/kuih kering” is not a defect.
food-001:foods-06.reason: “Biskuit” and “biskut” are the ordinary Indonesian and Malaysian forms for a biscuit in the stated dry baked-snack sense. Category boundaries with cookies and traditional dry cakes vary, but that does not impair this basic contrast.

health-001:health-01.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objections were supplied. The notes' caution about proving absolute preference is reasonable but does not undermine the well-established everyday status of either form.
health-001:health-01.reason: Obat and ubat are the ordinary, neutral general terms for medicine in Indonesia and Malaysia respectively. Both cover medicines taken internally or applied externally. The spelling-and-vowel contrast is useful and accurately classified as similar rather than same.

home-001:topic-02.historical_objection_assessment: The retailer-only evidence is narrow, but the broader preference claims themselves are linguistically sound. Malaysian kamar tidur is a nonpreferred synonym or Indonesian-influenced form, not an unresolved competitor. The limitation on context-free Indonesian kamar is correctly noted but irrelevant to the full form kamar tidur.
home-001:topic-02.reason: Kamar tidur is the normal Indonesian expression and bilik tidur the normal Malaysian expression for a bedroom. Bare kamar or bilik is common when context supplies the room type. Malaysian kamar tidur is understandable but does not eliminate the useful everyday national contrast.

corrections.historical_usage.malaysian.preferred: Peti sejuk is a safe standard and neutral choice. Peti ais is also common in everyday Malaysian usage, so do not claim that peti sejuk is uniquely preferred.
corrections.materially_misleading: No. The displayed Indonesian–Malaysian pair and relation are sound; only the Malaysian alternatives metadata needs correction.

home-001:topic-03.historical_objection_assessment: The objection about unresolved Malaysian preference is valid only against an exclusive preference claim; both peti sejuk and peti ais are established, natural terms. The objection to listing Malaysian kulkas is meritorious and requires removal. The food-versus-drink evidentiary observation is immaterial to the lexical sense.
home-001:topic-03.reason: Kulkas is the natural everyday Indonesian term, while peti sejuk is a standard and natural Malaysian term; Malaysian peti ais is also common. The contrast remains worth learning. Listing kulkas as an unqualified Malaysian alternative is misleading because it is characteristically Indonesian rather than an ordinary Malaysian Malay alternative.

The supplied sense is unnecessarily narrow and awkward: a window is not inherently a 'glass opening,' and both words can denote windows or wall openings without glass.

home-001:topic-05.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objections were supplied. Cross-border synonymy does not defeat the valid difference in ordinary default wording.
home-001:topic-05.reason: Tempat sampah is a natural default Indonesian expression for a household rubbish bin, while tong sampah is the normal Malaysian expression. Both forms may occur across the border, but the differing everyday defaults make the contrast useful and the proposed relation appropriate.

home-001:topic-06.historical_objection_assessment: The retailer evidence is narrow, but the substantive objection fails: both preferred forms accord with broad contemporary usage. Timba is a genuine overlapping Malaysian synonym, not a material blocker. The listing of ember as a Malaysian alternative is less secure, but it is peripheral and does not undermine the card.
home-001:topic-06.reason: For the specified handled household container, Indonesian ember and Malaysian baldi are natural, contemporary everyday choices. Timba is also common in Malaysia and can denote the same object, but that synonym does not invalidate the useful locale contrast or make baldi misleading.

home-001:topic-08.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied, and there is no evident semantic or usage defect.
home-001:topic-08.reason: Kursi in Indonesia and kerusi in Malaysia are the normal neutral words for a one-person seat with a back. The forms are closely related but observably different, making the contrast useful to learners.

places-001:places-01.historical_objection_assessment: The evidence reservations about exhaustive frequency do not create a genuine usage uncertainty. The proposed locale-specific choices and senses are well established.
places-001:places-01.reason: Kantor is the ordinary Indonesian place word for an office, while pejabat is the ordinary Malaysian word. Indonesian pejabat normally means an official or officeholder, which makes the contrast especially useful, although the displayed pair itself is best classified as different-common-word rather than false-friend because kantor and pejabat are not matching forms.

produce-001:produce-03.historical_objection_assessment: No historical objection was supplied. The fact that both words can also refer to unripe papaya in an appropriately modified or culinary context does not impair the card.
produce-001:produce-03.reason: Pepaya is the ordinary Indonesian name and betik the ordinary Malaysian name for papaya. Both cover the fruit generally; neither inherently marks ripeness, but the stated ripe-fruit referent is fully compatible with both words.

The objection to kendaraan pribadi and automobil as unqualified alternatives is also valid.
